chapter.name: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

questions.q: Which of these statements about the Iron Pillar of Delhi is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the pillar was probably erected first in front of the Udayagiri caves in Madhya Pradesh and brought to Delhi a few centuries later. The other three statements are the guide's own facts.
o: It has always stood at Mehrauli and was never moved
It weighs about 6 tonnes and is over 1,600 years old
It was dedicated to Vishnu and its inscriptions celebrate the king's achievements
It was erected during the reign of Chandragupta II

questions.q: Historians write 'II' after the name Chandragupta II because
questions.a: The chapter explains that an earlier Chandragupta, his grandfather, was called Chandragupta I. The Maurya king is a different person from a different dynasty, which is the confusion in the last option.
o: his grandfather was also called Chandragupta
he was the second son of Samudragupta
he ruled a second time after losing his throne
he came after Chandragupta Maurya

questions.q: Which empire, spread over the north and northwest of the Subcontinent, had started to weaken by the 3rd century CE, before the Guptas came to power?
questions.a: The chapter names the Kushana Empire. Maurya and Satavahana are earlier-chapter dynasties and the Vakatakas were the Guptas' neighbours, not the power that weakened.
o: The Kushana Empire
The Maurya Empire
The Satavahana kingdom
The Vakataka kingdom

questions.q: Gurleen's class visits Mehrauli. A classmate says, 'The pillar has stood in the open for 1,600 years, so all iron must be rust-proof if you leave it outside.' According to the chapter, what really protects the pillar?
questions.a: The 'Don't Miss Out' box says a unique thin layer, created by the special iron used and oxygen from the air, forms on the surface and protects it. The other options borrow real facts about the pillar (its dedication, weight and first site), but none of them is given as the protection.
o: A thin layer formed by the special iron and oxygen from the air
Its dedication to Vishnu, which kept the metal from corroding
Its 6-tonne weight, which kept the rain from reaching the iron
Its first place in front of the Udayagiri caves, which sheltered it

questions.q: Arjun copies the pillar's inscription into his notebook. It mentions a king called 'Chandra'. He writes, 'This must be Chandragupta Maurya, the king we studied earlier.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: The chapter says 'Chandra' on the pillar is identified with Chandragupta II and warns that he is not to be confused with Chandragupta Maurya. Chandragupta I and Samudragupta are other Gupta kings and are the near-miss options.
o: It has been identified with Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty
It is Chandragupta I, remembered for his coins and alliances
It is Samudragupta, who is praised in the Prayaga Prashasti
It is Chandragupta Maurya, since the pillar is dedicated to Vishnu

questions.q:
Read the statements about the pillar and the king.
1. The pillar was erected during the reign of Chandragupta II.
2. The pillar was first set up at Mehrauli, in front of the Udayagiri caves.
3. The inscription on the pillar celebrates the king's achievements.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: Udayagiri is in Madhya Pradesh, and Mehrauli is in Delhi, where the pillar was brought later. 1 and 3 are what the guide says.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Historians add the number II to the name Chandragupta II.
Reason (R): There was an earlier Gupta king named Chandragupta, his grandfather.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The numeral is there because an earlier Chandragupta, his grandfather, existed. R states exactly that reason, so it explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each place with what the chapter says about it.
Column A: 1. Mehrauli  2. Udayagiri caves  3. Pataliputra  4. Nandivardhana
Column B: a. Vakataka capital near present-day Nagpur  b. Gupta capital, present-day Patna  c. Probable first site of the pillar  d. Where the pillar stands today
questions.a: Mehrauli (Delhi) holds the pillar today; Udayagiri is where it probably stood first; Pataliputra is present-day Patna; Nandivardhana is near Nagpur. The distractors swap the two pillar sites, the two capitals, or both pairs.

questions.q: (a) Name the ruler in whose reign the Iron Pillar was erected and the god to whom it was dedicated. (b) The pillar probably stood first in front of the Udayagiri caves. What does this tell us about the pillar's journey?
questions.a: (a) Chandragupta II; dedicated to Vishnu. (b) It was moved: it was brought to Delhi a few centuries after it was erected, so its present place is not where it began.
s: Part (a): Chandragupta II and Vishnu
Part (b): it was brought to Delhi later from Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh

questions.q: (a) Which empire's weakening by the 3rd century CE set the stage for the Guptas? (b) How did that weakening help a new dynasty to rise?
questions.a: (a) The Kushana Empire. (b) New kingdoms emerged and a period of fresh consolidation began, and the Gupta dynasty became the new actor on this stage.
s: Part (a): names the Kushana Empire
Part (b): new kingdoms emerged, giving the Guptas room to rise

questions.q: The chapter says that art, architecture, literature and science flourished 'particularly during the time of Chandragupta II'. Name these four fields, and say what the word 'particularly' tells you about his reign compared with the rest of the dynasty.
questions.a: Art, architecture, literature and science. 'Particularly' means the flowering was strongest in his reign, so his time was a high point of the Gupta period.
s: Names the four fields
Reads "particularly" as his reign being the high point

questions.q: Differentiate between Chandragupta I and Chandragupta II on any two points mentioned in the chapter.
questions.a: Chandragupta I: the grandfather, remembered for coins and alliances that helped the early expansion. Chandragupta II: his grandson, also called Vikramaditya, a devotee of Vishnu, in whose reign the Iron Pillar was erected and the arts flourished.
s: Two correct points about Chandragupta I
Two correct points about Chandragupta II, kept separate

questions.q: (a) Name the god whom Chandragupta II followed and the mount (vahana) that often appears on his inscriptions. (b) How does your answer to (a) fit the Iron Pillar's dedication, and what does the inscription on the pillar celebrate?
questions.a: (a) Vishnu; Garuda. (b) The pillar was dedicated to Vishnu, the king's own god, and its inscription celebrates the king's achievements.
s: Part (a): Vishnu and Garuda
Part (b): pillar dedicated to Vishnu, so it matches; inscription celebrates the achievements

questions.q: Isha says, 'The Iron Pillar can tell us about Chandragupta II's reign, because it was erected then and its inscription celebrates his achievements.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter, and say what the pillar cannot tell us by itself.
questions.a: Yes, mostly. The chapter says the pillar was erected in his reign and that its inscription, which speaks of a king 'Chandra' identified with Chandragupta II, celebrates his achievements. But the pillar was probably moved from Udayagiri to Delhi, so its present place cannot show where he ruled, and an inscription that celebrates a king shows what was praised, not everything about his reign.
s: Verdict: agrees, with the reign and inscription as evidence
Notes the pillar was probably moved from Udayagiri, so its place is no proof of his territory
Notes that a celebrating inscription is one view of the reign

questions.q: Explain how the Guptas rose to power after the Kushana Empire weakened. Mention what the chapter says about their origin.
questions.a: By the 3rd century CE the Kushana Empire in the north and northwest weakened and new kingdoms emerged. The Guptas, whose origin is debated but who are widely believed to have started near present-day Uttar Pradesh as regional rulers, rose to prominence and built a powerful empire.
s: Kushana weakening and new kingdoms
Origin: near present-day Uttar Pradesh as regional rulers, theories differ
Rose to prominence and built a powerful empire

questions.q: Describe three facts the chapter gives about Chandragupta II.
questions.a: Any three: also called Vikramaditya; a devotee of Vishnu with Garuda appearing on inscriptions; the Iron Pillar was erected in his reign; art, architecture, literature and science flourished in his time; he surrounded himself with learned men, poets and artists.
s: First correct fact
Second correct fact
Third correct fact

questions.q: 'The Iron Pillar is both a marvel of science and a document of history.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Science: over 1,600 years old, about 6 tonnes, unrusted because of the special iron and a thin protective layer, which shows advanced metallurgy. History: it was erected in Chandragupta II's reign, dedicated to Vishnu, its inscription names 'Chandra' and celebrates the king's achievements, and it was probably moved from Udayagiri. So it tells us both what ancient craftsmen could do and who was ruling.
s: Science: age, weight and rust-resistance explained
History: reign, Vishnu, inscription and the move from Udayagiri
Draws the two together in a conclusion

questions.q: The chapter says the Kushana decline set the stage for 'a fresh period of consolidation'. Analyse how the early Guptas, up to Chandragupta II, built on that opening.
questions.a: The Kushana Empire weakened and new kingdoms emerged. The Guptas rose from near present-day Uttar Pradesh as regional rulers. Chandragupta I helped early expansion with coins and strategic alliances, laying a foundation. By Chandragupta II, art, architecture, literature and science were flourishing and the pillar was erected. Each step moved from a regional power to a remarkable empire.
s: Kushana weakening gave the opening
Guptas begin as regional rulers near present-day Uttar Pradesh
Chandragupta I: coins and alliances as foundation
Chandragupta II: flourishing of fields and the pillar
Links the stages into a clear line of growth

questions.q:
A Class 7 group from a Hyderabad school visits Mehrauli. The guide tells them the pillar is over 1,600 years old and weighs about 6 tonnes, and the inscription on it speaks of a king named 'Chandra'. Rohan says, 'That must be Chandragupta Maurya, whom we studied earlier.' Mehek says, 'The pillar stands in Delhi, so it proves the Guptas ruled Delhi.'
(a) Whom does the chapter identify 'Chandra' with, and whom does it warn us not to confuse him with?
(b) Where did the pillar probably stand first, and when was it brought to Delhi?
(c) Use your answer to (b) to test Mehek's claim.
(d) The school display needs one title: 'A marvel of metal' or 'A king's monument'. Which would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty; not Chandragupta Maurya of the Maurya dynasty. (b) In front of the Udayagiri caves in Madhya Pradesh; a few centuries later. (c) Because it was moved, its position in Delhi does not by itself show that the Guptas ruled Delhi; other evidence is needed. (d) Either, with reasons: 'A marvel of metal' rests on the unrusted pillar and its thin protective layer; 'A king's monument' rests on the reign, the Vishnu dedication and the inscription celebrating the king.
s: Part (a): Chandragupta II, not Chandragupta Maurya
Part (b): Udayagiri caves in Madhya Pradesh; brought a few centuries later
Part (c): moved, so Delhi is no proof of the Guptas' territory
Part (d): a title chosen and backed by a chapter fact

questions.q:
A Lucknow school runs a history quiz and reads out three clues without names. Clue W: 'By the 3rd century CE this empire of the north and northwest had begun to weaken.' Clue X: 'This Gupta king is remembered for his coins and strategic alliances.' Clue Y: 'This Gupta king is also called Vikramaditya, and a famous iron pillar was erected in his reign.'
(a) Name the empire in Clue W and the kings in Clues X and Y, with the numeral historians add to each Chandragupta.
(b) How are the kings in X and Y related, and why does the numeral exist?
(c) The round is titled 'How the Guptas rose'. How does Clue W connect to that title?
(d) The round has time for only two clues. Which clue would you drop, and what would the round lose?
questions.a: (a) The Kushana Empire; Chandragupta I (X); Chandragupta II (Y). (b) Grandfather and grandson; the numeral was added because there was an earlier Chandragupta. (c) The Kushana weakening let new kingdoms emerge, and the Gupta dynasty became the new actor. (d) Any clue, with a reason: dropping W loses the cause of the rise; dropping X loses the foundation of coins and alliances; dropping Y loses the high point (pillar, flowering of the arts), though Y is about the peak and not the rise.
s: Part (a): Kushana, Chandragupta I and II
Part (b): grandfather; numeral separates the two of the same name
Part (c): Kushana weakening gave the opening
Part (d): drops one clue and names what is lost

questions.q: Who composed the Prayaga Prashasti, the pillar inscription at Prayagraj that praises Samudragupta?
questions.a: The chapter names the court poet Harisena as the author. Kalidasa, Faxian and Varahamihira are other people of the Gupta age in the same chapter, but none wrote this inscription.
o: Harisena, the court poet
Kalidasa, the Sanskrit poet
Faxian, the Chinese traveller
Varahamihira of Ujjayini

questions.q: Samudragupta's ambition, according to Harisena, was to be 'dharani-bandha'. What does this mean?
questions.a: The chapter translates dharani-bandha as 'to unify the Earth'. The ashvamedha is the sacrifice ambitious kings sometimes performed, which is a separate idea.
o: To unify the Earth
To build the largest temple
To perform the ashvamedha yajna
To rule from the sea coast

questions.q: Which of these was NOT done by Samudragupta, according to the Prayaga Prashasti?
questions.a: The chapter says that many defeated kings were reinstated and offered tribute, and others submitted without protest. 'Every' and 'none' make the first option false.
o: He took over all defeated kingdoms and reinstated none
He fought many wars and defeated many kings
He reinstated some defeated kings who then paid him tribute
He supported art, learning and trade in his kingdom

questions.q: In a museum, Meera sees a gold coin with a king seated and playing a stringed instrument; the goddess Lakshmi is on the reverse. What does the chapter say it shows?
questions.a: Fig. 7.6 shows a seated Samudragupta playing the veena. The coin with the queen belongs to Chandragupta I, and the horse coin is the ashvamedha coin: these are the chapter's other coins.
o: Samudragupta portrayed as a veena player
Chandragupta I shown with his queen Kumaradevi
Samudragupta's sacrificial horse of the ashvamedha
Chandragupta II with his mount Garuda

questions.q: A coin in a school exhibit shows a sacrificial horse on one side and a queen holding a chauri (fly whisk) on the other. Which event was it minted to commemorate?
questions.a: The chapter says ashvamedha yajna was commemorated by minting special coins like the one in Fig. 7.7. Copper plates and Faxian's journey are separate topics in the chapter.
o: The ashvamedha yajna of an ambitious king
The grant of land recorded on a copper plate
The writing of the Prayaga Prashasti
A journey of Faxian across India

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Prayaga Prashasti.
1. It was written by Faxian during his travels in the early 5th century CE.
2. It praises Samudragupta, the father of Chandragupta II.
3. It records that some defeated kings were reinstated and paid tribute.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: Harisena, the court poet, wrote it; Faxian was a Chinese pilgrim who wrote a travelogue. Statements 2 and 3 are in the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Samudragupta fought many wars, defeating kings and expanding his empire.
Reason (R): According to Harisena, his ambition was to be dharani-bandha, 'to unify the Earth'.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The chapter says that 'to this end', the aim of unifying the Earth, he fought many wars. R gives the aim behind the wars in A, so it explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Which of the following is named in the Vishnu Purana's list of key Gupta regions?
questions.a: The Purana lists Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha. Kamarupa and Kanchipuram are neighbouring kingdoms and Ujjayini is where Varahamihira lived.
o: Magadha, approximately present-day Bihar
Kamarupa, ruled by the Varman dynasty
Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital in the south
Ujjayini, where Varahamihira lived

questions.q: (a) Name the pillar inscription that praises Samudragupta and its author. (b) Other than an inscription, name two kinds of source from this chapter that tell us about him or his empire.
questions.a: (a) The Prayaga Prashasti, by the court poet Harisena. (b) Any two kinds: coins (the veena coin, the ashvamedha coin) and a literary source such as the Vishnu Purana.
s: Part (a): Prayaga Prashasti and Harisena
Part (b): two valid non-inscription sources, such as coins and the Vishnu Purana

questions.q: (a) What happened to many kings whom Samudragupta defeated? (b) The chapter asks us to imagine moving an army of soldiers, elephants, horses and cooks. What does it suggest the tributary kings must have supplied?
questions.a: (a) Many were reinstated and offered tribute to him; some kingdoms were taken over. (b) Supplies and support to feed the whole army, since moving it needed a great deal of provisions.
s: Part (a): reinstated and paid tribute
Part (b): provisions and support for the army

questions.q: The Vishnu Purana lists Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha as key Gupta regions. How does this list differ from the empire at its peak?
questions.a: The Purana names a core in the Gangetic region. At its peak the empire was larger, covering most of present-day north and west India and parts of central and east India.
s: Purana list described as a core of named regions
Peak extent larger: north and west India, parts of central and east India

questions.q: Why were special coins minted after an ashvamedha yajna, and what did these coins show?
questions.a: The event was significant, so it was commemorated with special coins. Kings performed the yajna to build mighty empires and leave a legacy. The coin in the chapter shows the sacrificial horse, with the queen holding a chauri on the reverse.
s: Commemorated a significant event; ambitious kings sought a legacy
Coin showed the sacrificial horse (queen with chauri on the reverse)

questions.q: The book asks, 'Why do you think kings chose to proclaim their achievements in the form of inscriptions?' (a) Name one achievement of Samudragupta that Harisena's inscription proclaims. (b) Give one reason, in your own words, why a king would have such achievements cut in stone for the public.
questions.a: (a) Any one: he fought many wars and defeated kings; he supported art, learning and trade. (b) A reasoned inference, for example: stone lasts for a long time and many people can see it, so the achievements are remembered and the king's power is announced. The book leaves this question for the reader.
s: Part (a): one achievement from the Prashasti
Part (b): a sensible reason such as lasting, public record

questions.q: Pooja says, 'Samudragupta was a patron of the arts as well as a warrior.' Do you agree? Support your answer with two pieces of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Warrior: he fought many wars and defeated kings. Patron: Harisena wrote that he supported art, learning and trade, and one of his coins shows him playing the veena. The claim is supported by both sources.
s: Verdict: agrees
Warrior evidence: many wars and defeated kings
Patron evidence: Prashasti on art, learning and trade, or the veena coin

questions.q: Explain why the Vishnu Purana alone cannot be used to say how large the Gupta Empire was at its peak.
questions.a: It names only key regions (Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa, Magadha and the surrounding regions). At its peak the empire covered most of north and west India with parts of central and east India, which is larger. So a single source gives only part of the picture and others are needed.
s: States what the Purana lists
States the larger peak extent
Concludes more than one source is needed

questions.q: Read the two coins as evidence: one shows Samudragupta with a veena, another shows a sacrificial horse. What does each tell us about him, and what do they show together?
questions.a: The veena coin shows him as a patron of art. The horse coin recalls an ashvamedha yajna, which ambitious kings performed to build empires. Together they show a warrior-king who also loved the arts.
s: Veena coin: patron of art
Horse coin: ashvamedha and imperial ambition
Combines the two into one picture of the king

questions.q: 'No single source tells the whole story of Samudragupta and his empire.' Justify this statement using the Prayaga Prashasti, the coins and the Vishnu Purana.
questions.a: Prashasti: written by the court poet Harisena, it tells of his ambition to unify the Earth, many wars, reinstated kings and support for art, learning and trade. Coins: one shows him playing the veena and another recalls an ashvamedha yajna, which add the arts and imperial ambition. Vishnu Purana: names Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa, Magadha and 'surrounding regions', but at its peak the empire was larger. Each source adds something the others do not, so they need to be read together.
s: Prashasti: what it tells
Coins: what they add
Purana: regions named and the larger peak extent
Conclusion: sources need to be combined

questions.q: Compare the three ways Samudragupta dealt with the kings he met: taking kingdoms over, reinstating kings who paid tribute, and kings who submitted without protest. Analyse how these helped him build an empire.
questions.a: Some kingdoms were taken over, which added land directly to the empire. Others were reinstated and paid tribute, which brought wealth and supplies without ruling them directly. Some kings submitted at once, fearing his might, so no war was needed. Together, force and fear produced a large empire and tributary kings could also provide for his huge army.
s: Taking over described
Reinstating with tribute described
Peaceful submission described
Analysis: how each added to the empire
Link to supplying the army

questions.q:
Vihaan, a Class 7 student in Prayagraj, makes a chart of three sources. P: the stone inscription in his city, written by a court poet in praise of a Gupta king. Q: a gold coin showing a horse on one side and a queen holding a fly whisk (chauri) on the other. R: a line from an old text that says the dynasty will rule Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha and 'all the surrounding regions'. He writes at the bottom, 'The Gupta Empire had four regions.'
(a) Name P and its author, and say what event the coin Q commemorates.
(b) What does Q show about the kings who issued it, and which fact told by P agrees with this?
(c) Why is Vihaan's conclusion at the bottom incomplete?
(d) His teacher lets him keep only one of P and Q for a stall called 'What kind of king was he?'. Which should he keep, and why?
questions.a: (a) The Prayaga Prashasti, by Harisena; an ashvamedha yajna. (b) Ambitious kings performed it to build mighty empires and leave a legacy; P agrees, as it says Samudragupta wanted to unify the Earth and fought many wars. (c) R says 'surrounding regions' too, and at its peak the empire covered most of north and west India with parts of central and east India. (d) Either, with a reason: P gives wars, ambition and patronage; Q gives a vivid sign of imperial ambition in a single object.
s: Part (a): Prayaga Prashasti, Harisena, ashvamedha
Part (b): imperial ambition, agreeing with the aim of unifying the Earth
Part (c): more than four regions at the peak
Part (d): chooses P or Q with a reason

questions.q:
A Patna school plans a role play of a Gupta army marching east. The planning sheet lists soldiers, elephants, horses, cooks and other support staff. Plan 1: carry all supplies from the capital's stores, so that no king on the way can refuse. Plan 2: carry part of the supplies and ask the kings of the region to provide the rest.
(a) What happened to many kings whom Samudragupta defeated, according to the Prashasti?
(b) Which kings does the chapter suggest were asked to provide for such an army? (The book offers this as imagination, not as a record.)
(c) Which plan is closer to the chapter's reasoning?
(d) Plan 1 is safer if a king refuses. Decide which plan you would back, giving one reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) They were reinstated and offered tribute to him. (b) The tributary kings. (c) Plan 2, because the chapter reasons that the tributary kings must have been asked to provide. (d) Either, with a reason: Plan 2, because kings who kept their thrones paid tribute and others submitted fearing his might; Plan 1, because refusal is possible and moving supplies in advance is safer, though the heavy load is a cost.
s: Part (a): reinstated and paid tribute
Part (b): tributary kings
Part (c): Plan 2 with the chapter's reasoning
Part (d): a plan chosen with a reason from the chapter

questions.q: Why did the Chinese traveller Faxian journey to India in the early 5th century CE?
questions.a: The chapter says his pilgrimage was for sacred Buddhist sites, scholars and manuscripts. Trade and astronomy are real topics of the chapter but not his purpose.
o: To visit Buddhist holy sites and collect manuscripts
To trade in textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones
To serve as an envoy at the court of Chandragupta II
To study the motion of the Sun, Moon and planets

questions.q: What is the name of Faxian's travelogue quoted in the chapter?
questions.a: The excerpt is from A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms (AD 399-414), translated by J. Legge. The other three are Gupta-age works by Indian authors.
o: A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms
Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira
Aryabhatiya of Aryabhata
Meghadutam of Kalidasa

questions.q: In the chapter, the 'chandalas' were
questions.a: The chapter says Faxian describes the harsh treatment of the chandalas, regarded as outcastes. The other options are groups in the excerpt who are described as prosperous.
o: outcastes who lived outside the city limits
wealthy Vaishya families who ran houses of charity
salaried guards and attendants in the king's service
foreign merchants living in beautiful city homes

questions.q: Which of the following does Faxian's excerpt say about the people of the cities he visited?
questions.a: The excerpt says guards and attendants have salaries. It says people need not register households, farmers of royal land pay a portion of grain, and heads of Vaishya families establish charity houses.
o: The king's guards and attendants receive salaries
All townspeople must register their households with officials
Farmers of royal land pay nothing to the king
Charity houses are run by the king's officers alone

questions.q: Kabir reads only the excerpt and writes, 'Everyone in Gupta society was happy and well treated.' Which point from the chapter shows his conclusion is incomplete?
questions.a: The chapter itself notes Faxian's description of the chandalas' treatment. The other options are not given as facts in the book, so they are inventions rather than evidence.
o: Faxian also reports the harsh treatment of chandalas
The excerpt was written by Harisena to praise the king
Farmers of royal land paid no grain to the king at all
Heads of Vaishya families refused to care for the sick

questions.q: Two groups in a Class 7 read the same Faxian excerpt. One says it shows a prosperous society, the other says it shows a caring society. Which idea from the chapter does this show?
questions.a: The chapter says a group of historians may examine the same source and draw varied interpretations, which is why they look for more sources. 'Must' in the second option is the trap, since both readings fit the lines.
o: Historians can read one source in varied ways
One of the two groups must have made a mistake
A translated source cannot be used by historians
Only royal inscriptions allow different readings

questions.q:
Read the statements about Faxian.
1. His travelogue has survived to this day.
2. He visited India in the early 5th century CE.
3. He recorded his experiences mainly for the people of the Gupta capital.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 is false: he recorded his observations for the people of his homeland, China. Statements 1 and 2 are in the chapter.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Faxian's travelogue has survived to this day.
Reason (R): Faxian was a Chinese traveller who visited India in the early 5th century CE.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. Who he was and when he came do not explain why the text has survived, so R is not the explanation.
o: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Faxian writes that the people 'have no need to register households or attend to officials'. (a) What does this line say about how closely people were recorded? (b) Which other line of his excerpt tells us how the king collected from farmers of royal land?
questions.a: (a) Ordinary households did not have to register or go to officials, so people were not closely recorded by officials, as he saw it. (b) 'Those who farm royal land pay a portion of their grain.'
s: Part (a): no registering of households or attending to officials
Part (b): farmers of royal land pay a portion of their grain

questions.q: (a) Give any two reasons for Faxian's pilgrimage. (b) Name his travelogue and the people for whom he wrote it.
